idiom_name: TCPServer#accept loop + thread per connection; TCPSocket.new as connector
implementation_notes: Ruby's stdlib gives the two roles directly—TCPServer.new + accept is the acceptor and TCPSocket.new is the synchronous connector—but it has no handler factory; the classic structure hands each socket to a per-connection object or thread. accept_nonblock accepts without blocking the caller, returning :wait_readable on EAGAIN; wrap it with IO.select. For a non-blocking connector use Socket#connect_nonblock and handle IO::WaitWritable, or use an evented stack such as Falcon or Async::HTTP::Server. Use TCPServer.open with a block to ensure the listening socket is closed on exit.
code_sketch:
server = TCPServer.new("0.0.0.0", 8080)
loop do
  client = server.accept
  Thread.start(client) { |socket| handle_session(socket) }
end
# connector: socket = TCPSocket.new(host, 8080)
pitfalls: Unbounded Thread.start per accept exhausts memory under load; use a thread pool.
Blocking accept/read freezes the calling thread; use accept_nonblock with IO.select or an evented server.
Shared mutable state across connection threads needs a Mutex/Queue; give each thread its own connection object.
TCPSocket.new performs DNS resolution and connection synchronously; for async-style code use Socket#connect_nonblock with IO.select or an evented client.
Closing a socket while another thread reads raises IOError: 'stream closed'; use a Queue to signal shutdown order.
